design_detail: Qualitative interview study by a single author (School of Sociology and Social Policy, Queen's University Belfast; Substance Use & Misuse 40:1461-1477). Face-to-face, semi-structured, in-depth interviews of 1 to 2 hours, taped and transcribed, with 98 people who currently or formerly used ecstasy in Northern Ireland, October 1997 to November 1998 (106 interviewed; 8 interviews discarded because of recording or transcription problems). Eligibility was any use of ecstasy, with criteria narrowed during the study to reach people outside Belfast and people who had stopped using, and to avoid over-representing groups such as middle-class students. Recruitment through announcements in shops and health centres, advertisements in a club and music magazine, local agencies (youth programmes, universities, sexually transmitted disease clinics, gay and lesbian outreach, young offender programmes, drug services), the interviewers' own contacts and street sources, snowball referral and paid gatekeepers (10 pounds per referral and completed interview, usually up to six); clubs were deliberately not used. The interview covered first, last and usual use, positive and negative experiences, rituals and norms, health and other items; sexuality and sexual risk are reported as themes illustrated by quotations labelled with respondent number, sex and age. Counts are given for the sample (Tables 1 and 2) but not for any finding, and the method of analysis is not described.
can_establish: How these Northern Irish respondents described MDMA's effects on sensuality, sexual desire and sexual performance, and the kinds of sexual risk they reported during MDMA episodes, in 1997 and 1998.
cannot_establish: How common any of these experiences is among people who use MDMA (no finding is counted and the sample is purposive), whether MDMA rather than the alcohol, cannabis or other drugs taken in the same episodes, or individual differences in sexual interest, produced them, or whether sexual risk is greater with MDMA than without it (condoms were rarely used without drugs either).

sample.recruitment: Community, several methods (see design detail). Of the 98: 18% recruited by snowball referral, 26% by one of nine paid gatekeepers, 29% learned of the study through one of its employees and 27% from an advertisement. Each received a music or book gift certificate printed as $15 (US $27) (pp. 1463-1464).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Any lifetime use of ecstasy. After about 4 months, when most respondents were from Belfast, criteria were narrowed to people outside Belfast or people who had stopped using, and at other times adjusted to avoid over-representation, for example of middle-class students (p. 1463, footnote d).
sample.demographics: 69% men and 31% women; age 17 to 45 (mean 25, median 24, mode 23); 16% gay or bisexual (self-defined); 50% lived in Belfast, 46% elsewhere in Northern Ireland and 4% outside it; 49% working class, 46% middle class and 5% between (self-defined); 57% employed (p. 1464; Table 1, p. 1465).
sample.attrition: 8 of 106 interviews (8%) discarded for recording or transcription problems (p. 1463); the 12 pilot interviews were kept (p. 1464).
sample.selection_effects: Purposive sample built through agencies, contacts and paid referral, deliberately avoiding clubs; long and heavy use was common (44% had used ecstasy on at least 100 occasions). How many respondents discussed sex, and how many had sex during MDMA episodes, is not reported.

exposure.measurement: Self-report in the interview. The author notes that tablet content varies, so effects attributed to MDMA refer to what respondents believed they had taken (p. 1463, footnote c).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Lifetime: 44% at least 100 separate episodes. Past 6 months: 8% no use, 50% less than once a month, 37% one to four times a month; about half had used within 2 weeks of the interview. First use at mean age 21 (median 20, range 13 to 35) (p. 1465; Table 2, p. 1466). Amounts per episode not reported.
exposure.polysubstance: All had used cannabis (32% daily in the past 6 months); 90% had used LSD or mushrooms and 93% amphetamines; 45% cocaine or crack and 11% heroin; 84% drank beer, lager, ale or stout weekly (mean 16 pints a week among them); 60% smoked at least 20 cigarettes a day (p. 1465; Table 2, p. 1466). Alcohol and cannabis were often used in the same episodes, and the author says their interactions with MDMA could not be examined (p. 1473).

comparison.controls: None. Respondents compared, in their own words, sex with and without MDMA, MDMA with alcohol, and their reactions with friends'.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Sexual interest, relationship status and sexual behaviour without drugs were not measured systematically; the author suggests individual differences in sexual interest may explain the diverse accounts (p. 1470).

outcomes.instruments: Semi-structured interview guide, piloted on the first 12 respondents and slightly revised, covering use, experiences, rituals and norms, health and other items; demographic and drug-history questions at the end (p. 1464). Questions about sexual risk are mentioned (p. 1473), but the sexuality questions are not reproduced.
outcomes.validity_norms: Not applicable. No coding procedure, coder agreement, saturation criterion or member checking is described.
outcomes.operationalization: Sexual risk is the author's category (multiple partners, partners who were strangers or acquaintances, sex without a condom); the author notes that several respondents needed the question clarified and may not regard these behaviours as risky (pp. 1462, 1473).
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Not applicable. Four interviewers (two women and two men, two of them the project directors) trained for 2 weeks (p. 1464).

analysis.effect_sizes: None; themes without counts. The quantifiers used are a slight majority (sensuality or deep emotions rather than sexual desire, p. 1467), the majority (sensuality and emotional closeness often without sexual activity, p. 1470), and several, some, a number of or a few elsewhere.
analysis.preregistration_detail: No protocol is mentioned; the interview topics are described in an earlier report (McElrath and McEvoy, 1999, Ecstasy Use in Northern Ireland, as cited on p. 1464).
analysis.selective_reporting: No finding is counted. Quotations carry respondent numbers, which show some themes resting on a few people (respondent 022 is quoted or cited four times, on pp. 1468, 1470, 1471 and 1472, and 018 three times).
analysis.power: Not applicable; no saturation criterion is given.

interpretation_gap.results_show: A slight majority described MDMA mainly as bringing sensuality and emotional closeness rather than sexual desire. Some men who tried to have sex described being unable to get an erection or to ejaculate, reportedly more often among men aged 25 or younger; other men and women described heightened desire and very good sex, and a few used MDMA as a sexual aid with a partner. Some described multiple partners, one-night stands and next-day regret, mostly younger respondents; condoms were rarely used during MDMA episodes with intercourse, but few respondents used them when no drugs had been taken either; views on whether MDMA or alcohol led to more sexual risk were mixed.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract says most respondents reported closeness without desire for penetrative sex, where the findings say a slight majority (pp. 1461, 1467). It says gay and bisexual women in particular had used MDMA for sexual enhancement, while the Discussion says the small number of gay and bisexual women in the sample prohibits accurate conclusions (p. 1473). It calls sexual risk taking prevalent among those who had sex during MDMA episodes, without saying how many had sex or took risks, and without the finding that condom use was also rare when no drugs were taken (p. 1472). The statements that heavy drinkers were as likely as others to attempt sex and that feelings did not differ by lifetime use (p. 1471) are impressions without counts.

timeline.event: Buffum and Moser, as cited here: MDMA did not increase the desire to initiate sex but enhanced receptivity to being sexual (p. 1462); not read.

Beck and Rosenbaum, book on MDMA experiences, as cited here: feelings of emotional and physical closeness, and frequent sex with multiple partners in the 1980s Dallas club scene (pp. 1468, 1473-1474); not read.

Zemishlany, Aizenberg and Weizman, retrospective interviews of 35 people in Israel about sex after MDMA: all reported more desire; erections worse in 8 of 20 men and better in 8; orgasm delayed in 16 men and 6 of 15 women.

replication.where_it_stands: Qualitative and survey accounts from the 1980s and 1990s agree that MDMA is often experienced as sensual and emotionally close rather than sexual, with erectile difficulty for some men and heightened desire for others. None of the sources read measures how often these occur among people who use MDMA now, and the author says the scene may have changed since 1997 and 1998 (p. 1474).

funding.affiliations_note: Single author, a Reader in the School of Sociology and Social Policy, Queen's University Belfast (pp. 1461, 1476). The interviews were part of a project with two project directors described in a 1999 report (McElrath and McEvoy, Ecstasy Use in Northern Ireland, Stationery Office, as cited); its funder is not named here.

what_would_settle_it: A survey of a defined population of people who use MDMA, with validated measures of sexual function and of sexual behaviour on occasions with MDMA, with alcohol alone and with neither, recording what else was taken, to show how often each experience occurs and whether risk differs from occasions without MDMA.

domains.domain: Research design appropriate to the question (qualitative appraisal, CASP-style)
domains.note: In-depth interviews suit a question about how people perceive MDMA's effects on sexuality and risk.

Purposive multi-method sampling, adjusted during the study to diversify the sample, with paid gatekeepers and clubs avoided for safety; no saturation account; how many respondents spoke about sex is not given.
Trained interviewers, a piloted guide, private settings, taped and transcribed; but the sexuality questions are not reproduced and 8 of 106 interviews were lost.

29% learned of the study through a project employee and some were recruited through interviewers' own contacts; the author notes that researchers and respondents saw risk differently, but gives no account of how the interviewers may have shaped answers.
Confidentiality and anonymity assured, respondents identified by number, an incentive given and clubs avoided for safety; no ethics approval or consent procedure is mentioned.
How the transcripts were analysed (coding, theme development, who coded, any checks) is not described at all.
Themes are illustrated with attributed quotations, but quantifiers such as most, a slight majority and several have no counts, and the abstract states findings more strongly than the text.
The author states plainly that the data are from Northern Ireland in 1997 and 1998 and may not apply now (p. 1474).

risk_of_bias.reasoning: Appraised with the editors' qualitative checklist. A large interview study with careful, diversified recruitment and a frank statement of its time and place, but with no description of how the transcripts were analysed and no counts behind its quantified statements, so the overall judgment follows the analysis domain. It may be cited for the range of experiences described in this Northern Irish sample of 1997 and 1998: closeness without sexual desire, erectile difficulty for some men, heightened desire and use as a sexual aid for others, and sexual risk episodes with regret. It should not be cited for how often any of these occurs, or as showing that MDMA increases sexual risk.

key_findings.finding: Sample: 98 people who currently or formerly used ecstasy in Northern Ireland, interviewed October 1997 to November 1998 (106 interviewed, 8 interviews discarded); 69% men; age 17 to 45 (mean 25); 16% gay or bisexual; 44% had used ecstasy on at least 100 occasions and 92% in the past 6 months.
key_findings.locator: Methods, 1st paragraph (p. 1463) and 3rd paragraph (p. 1464); Description of Respondents, 1st paragraph (p. 1464) and 2nd and 3rd paragraphs (p. 1465); Table 1 (p. 1465); Table 2 (p. 1466)

key_findings.finding: Closeness rather than sex: a slight majority described ecstasy as more associated with sensuality or deep emotions than with sexual desire; several men described wanting to hold someone, be with others or dance rather than have sex, and several women described sensual closeness without wanting penetrative sex.
key_findings.locator: Findings > Feelings of Sensuality or Emotional Closeness, 1st and 2nd paragraphs (p. 1467) and 3rd paragraph (p. 1468); block quotations not counted as paragraphs

key_findings.finding: Erections: some men who tried to have sex during ecstasy episodes described being unable to get an erection or to ejaculate, which appeared to affect men aged 25 or younger more often than men aged 26 to 38; for these men the author says it was physical inability, not a preference for sensuality.

Heightened desire: other men and women described strongly enhanced desire and very good sex on ecstasy, usually in private homes after clubs or at house parties; a few used ecstasy as a sexual aid with a steady partner, some felt more open to new forms of sex, and some women described exploring bisexuality.
key_findings.locator: Findings > Sexual Arousal, 2nd paragraph (p. 1468), 3rd to 7th paragraphs (p. 1469) and 8th paragraph (p. 1470)

key_findings.finding: Two patterns: the author summarizes that the majority described sensuality, empathy and closeness often without sexual activity, while an apparently distinct group described more desire and sexual fulfilment, possibly reflecting general differences in sexual interest; heavy drinkers were described as just as likely as light drinkers or non-drinkers to attempt sex, and feelings did not appear to differ between people with at least 100 uses and those with few (no counts).
key_findings.locator: Findings > Sexual Arousal, 10th paragraph (p. 1470) and 12th paragraph (p. 1471)

key_findings.finding: Gay and bisexual women appeared more likely than other respondents to use MDMA for sexual enhancement, but the author says their small number in the sample prohibits accurate conclusions.
key_findings.locator: Discussion > MDMA As a Sexual 'Aid', 1st paragraph

key_findings.finding: Sexual risk: several respondents who had sex during ecstasy episodes described behaviours carrying infection risk, more often those aged about 18 to 25: multiple partners and one-night stands with strangers or distant acquaintances; a number of men and women voiced next-day regret. (Regret is not an infection-risk behaviour.)
key_findings.locator: Findings > Sexual Risk Behaviors, 1st to 3rd paragraphs

key_findings.finding: Condoms: condom use was rare during ecstasy episodes that involved intercourse, but few respondents used condoms during sex when no drugs had been taken either; some used them with strangers but not with partners.

MDMA against alcohol: asked which brought more sexual risk, respondents were mixed; some said risk was greater on ecstasy, others that alcohol was far more likely to lead to risk and that they felt more in control on ecstasy; because a number of respondents took alcohol and other substances in the same episodes, the author says their effects are difficult to disentangle. (Source: 'difficult to disentangle', p. 1472, not 'could not be'.)
key_findings.locator: Findings > Sexual Risk Behaviors, 7th and 8th paragraphs

key_findings.finding: Limitations stated: the data are from 1997 and 1998 and the scene has probably changed (tablet prices, by anecdotal report, fell from about 10 to 5 pounds; researchers in England report more alcohol use in clubs, and the author says similar changes are possible in Northern Ireland), so it is unclear whether the findings apply now; prospective data, with the timing of substance use and sex, might be needed. (pp. 1473-1474: the alcohol change is England's and only 'possible' locally; 'might be needed'.)
key_findings.locator: Discussion > The Role of MDMA, Other Drugs, and Sexual Behavior, 2nd paragraph (p. 1472, continuing on p. 1473); Limitations of the Study and Suggestions for Future Research, 1st paragraph (p. 1474)

key_findings.finding: Context from footnotes: clubs were not used for recruitment because local folklore tied some paramilitary groups to clubs and recruiting there might have raised suspicion and put respondents and researchers at risk; respondents said some clubs turned off water taps in toilets, and in several clubs only bottled water was sold; respondents said they recognised people on MDMA by large black pupils, clenched teeth, an 'irregular' jaw formation and extreme friendliness, particularly with strangers. (Footnote e says 'local folklore suggests', not 'reported links'.)
key_findings.locator: Footnote e (p. 1464); footnote h (p. 1466); footnote i (p. 1467)

reporting_issues.issue: The method of analysis of the transcripts is not reported, and no finding is counted; the abstract turns the findings' slight majority (p. 1467) into most respondents (p. 1461).
reporting_issues.consequence: How themes were derived cannot be judged, and the abstract's quantifiers should not be cited.

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract singles out gay and bisexual women as having used MDMA for sexual enhancement, which the Discussion says their small number does not allow to be concluded (p. 1473).
reporting_issues.consequence: The subgroup statement should not be cited as a finding.

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract calls sexual risk taking prevalent among those who had sex during MDMA episodes, but the paper gives neither the number who had sex during episodes nor the number reporting risk, and reports that condom use was also rare when no drugs were taken.
reporting_issues.consequence: Neither the prevalence of sexual risk nor any difference from sex without MDMA can be taken from this paper.

reporting_issues.issue: Table 2's past-6-month categories (no use 8%, less than once a month 50%, one to four times a month 37%) sum to 95%; the other 5% are not described, and the 77% described as currently using MDMA are not defined, although 92% had used in the past 6 months.
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; frequency of use cannot be fully described from the table.

reporting_issues.issue: The incentive is printed as a $15 (US $27) gift certificate, where the conversion implies 15 pounds sterling.

No supplement.

disagreements.reviewer: moderate rather than minor: Domain: abstract. Moderate rather than minor: three abstract statements go beyond the text (most for a slight majority; gay and bisexual women singled out although the Discussion says their numbers prohibit conclusions; risk 'prevalent' without counts and without condoms being rare without drugs too), and the abstract is the part most often cited.
disagreements.resolution: The card's scale has no 'moderate' (none, minor, substantial, severe); the AI co-editor sets 'substantial', since the second reader found the summary's conclusions going beyond the data in several places.
